articles.title: The FAA is finally ditching floppy disks
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced the FAA is replacing 1980s floppy disks with the E-IDS digital system, using legacy tech debt to deflect from aviation crises.
articles.body: It’s the year 2026 and the Federal Aviation Administration is still running critical pieces of American airspace on 3.5-inch magnetic floppy disks. But those technology artifacts could be headed for the dustbin after Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced an effort to ditch floppy disks in favor of a new digital system. Duffy announced Thursday that the FAA is rolling out the Enterprise – Information Display System (E-IDS) to replace four legacy setups across more than 400 air traffic control facilities. E-IDS aggregates real-time weather alerts, equipment outages, restricted airspace changes, and pilot reports onto a modern digital dashboard, replacing manual workflows and archaic physical storage media. Upgrades have already kicked off at five sites — including control hubs in Atlantic City, Nashville, Rochester, Atlanta, and Salt Lake City — with a targeted rollout across 435 facilities by the end of 2028. “Good news America: floppy disks are out, 21st century tech is in,” Duffy said in a release. [Media: Duffy, a former reality TV star and Fox Business host, has been using floppy disks as a scapegoat for the air travel disruptions that have plagued the country for years now. He waves them around during speeches or TV interviews, while highlighting that the FAA still uses “copper wires and floppy disks” as a symbol of government obsolescence. Indeed, our air traffic control system is deeply out of date, especially when held up alongside the more modern approaches of other nations. A Government Accountability Office report from September 2024 found that 90 percent of the nation’s critical air traffic control infrastructure was due or past due for a “technology refresh.” Nearly half of the 138 systems surveyed were “considered unsustainable” or “potentially unsustainable” due to shortfalls in funding, insufficient maintenance expertise, or even a lack of spare parts. But E-IDS is not an overnight breakthrough cooked up in a single executive sprint; it’s an existing FAA contract that has spent years working through procurement, safety validation, testing, and vendor timelines. The initial contract for E-IDS was awarded to Leidos, a defense contractor headquartered in Reston, Virginia, by the FAA back in August 2020, during the first Trump administration. The scope of the problem was understood, even back then. But since then, it has gotten much worse. The FAA has faced backlash in recent years over ground stops, close calls on runways (including one involving President Donald Trump), chronic burnout among air traffic controllers, and high-profile software meltdowns, like the 2023 NOTAM outage. Duffy is clearly trying the frame the system’s problems around relics like the floppy disk, as if obsolete tech is the only reason for the disruptions. But as we’ve noted before, it’s a much bigger problem than just the systems themselves. Replacing an information system with digital panels is relatively low-hanging fruit compared to the systemic crises plaguing American aviation, such as a crippling deficit of thousands of certified professional controllers. Duffy has been lobbying Congress for an additional $30 billion, on top of the $12.5 billion “down payment” he got in 2025, for his ATC modernization plan. Under Duffy, the USDOT has made a big deal about recruiting gamers, specifically, to take on these roles. And the administration is also relying on its tech oligarch allies, including Elon Musk and Peter Thiel, to help them clean up the mess — even if they happen to make it worse in the process.

articles.title: Banks brace for tighter oversight from US Congress after Democrats sweep
articles.summary: By Nupur Anand, Tatiana Bautzer and Michelle Price NEW YORK, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Wall Street banks were bracing on Wednesday for heightened scrutiny after Demo...
articles.body:
By Nupur Anand, Tatiana Bautzer and Michelle Price

NEW YORK, Nov 5 (Reuters) - Wall Street banks were bracing on Wednesday for heightened scrutiny after Democrats took control of the US Congress, with executives and analysts predicting lawmakers would investigate cost-of-living issues and summon bank chiefs to testify.

Democrats are already preparing to investigate business dealings by President ‌Donald Trump and members of his administration. Banking sources said the industry also expects that the massive shift in Washington could allow lawmakers to advance efforts to crack down ‌on artificial-intelligence-driven fraud.

Attorneys and analysts widely expect Democrats will probe consumer finance practices that may raise customer costs, such as junk fees, predatory lending and mortgages. One banking source said Democrats may also probe whether a pullback on regulation and ​oversight has hurt customers or weakened lenders. Two other people said lenders expect to spend more time responding to staff inquiries and preparing for hearings.

"There would certainly be attempts to bring back some of the restrictions on banks," said Peter Ricchiuti, professor at Tulane's Freeman School of Business. "Consumer protection initiatives might be brought back to life."

In 2024, Wall Street bank CEOs from Jamie Dimon at JPMorgan Chase to David Solomon at Goldman Sachs congratulated Trump and welcomed the Republican as a business-friendly president.

Over the past two years, the industry has scored major capital relief and other big policy wins from Trump's regulators. Yet Trump has also targeted some ‌banks, accusing the industry of refusing services to customers on political grounds ⁠and personally suing JPMorgan. The banks have denied Trump's claims.

Now, attorneys and advisors said the industry is trying to figure out how to handle Democrats who will assume control of both houses of the US Congress in January, handing them investigative staffs and subpoena power. Many financial services firms have been ⁠conducting risk assessments of their dealings with the Trump administration and identifying areas that could draw congressional interest, they said. Some are also already engaging with senior Democratic lawmakers, they added.

"The period between now and the end of the year I consider to be one of the most critical periods because you can do a lot of pre-emptive work," Tom Perez, a partner at the law firm Mayer Brown, said at a Washington ​event ​on congressional oversight last week. Companies should check for any pending congressional inquiries that they may not have addressed, ​he added.
authors: By Nupur Anand, Tatiana Bautzer and Michelle Price

articles.title: OpenAI rebrands data centers as ‘compute campuses,’ unveils new framework
articles.summary: OpenAI unveiled a new framework Thursday for building data centers, which it appears to be rebranding as “compute campuses” following the recent groundswell of opposition to the server warehouses powering the AI boom. The ChatGPT maker said it is committed to paying the full cost of electricity and infrastructure associated with its projects while providing…
articles.body:
OpenAI unveiled a new framework Thursday for building data centers, which it appears to be rebranding as “compute campuses” following the recent groundswell of opposition to the server warehouses powering the AI boom.

The ChatGPT maker said it is committed to paying the full cost of electricity and infrastructure associated with its projects while providing financial assurances in case they are reduced or canceled.

It is also pledging to prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, publish information about electricity and water use and not rely on nondisclosure agreements (NDA), which have limited public information about data center deals.

“The investments that help America compete globally can also help communities prosper locally,” it wrote in a press release. “That starts with giving residents a say while plans can still change and a way to hold developers accountable for delivering on their commitments.”

“That’s what we’re committing to at the campuses we own and operate, and what we believe people should be able to count on wherever AI infrastructure is built across the country,” the company added.

OpenAI also laid out a policy blueprint, suggesting voluntary commitments from companies are an “important starting point” while urging policymakers to establish “clear rules.”

Major tech companies, including OpenAI, signed on to a White House pledge in May, committing to cover the cost of building new data centers — though the agreement was not legally binding.

The ChatGPT maker’s proposals are largely aligned with its own commitments. It suggested state utility commissions should require large electricity customers to cover the costs they add to the grid and shield other customers if a project falls through.

The AI firm also called for public reporting on water, energy, noise and hiring, as well as restrictions on the use of NDAs. And it urged Congress to help speed up grid transmission upgrades and restore tax incentives for clean electricity.

OpenAI referred to the projects as “compute campuses” in the release in an apparent effort to rebrand data centers.

Tuesday’s election underscored the deep unpopularity of data centers, which helped carry Democrats to victory in key races. Americans also voted in favor of restricting data center construction in dozens of ballot measures across the country.

Other major tech firms, including Amazon, Meta and Microsoft, have similarly pledged to ensure their data center projects won’t raise consumers electricity bills, are increasingly water efficient and boost the local workforce.

articles.title: US government warns of 'ongoing cyber threat' amid mass hacks of industrial retail and military freezers | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A joint U.S. government statement says the hacks are affecting the food, transportation, and healthcare industries after reports of global mass hacks.
articles.body:
The U.S. government is warning of an “ongoing cyber threat” facing industrial refrigeration units, after reports of cyberattacks targeting freezers and fridges in supermarkets around the world, U.S. military bases, and at least one blood bank.

U.S. cybersecurity agency CISA, the FBI, and several other federal government departments warned in a joint statement on Thursday that hackers are targeting and compromising internet-connected refrigeration and cold chain monitoring systems in grocery stores and cold storage facilities. The statement said that the hacks are hitting critical infrastructure, such as the food, agriculture, transportation, and medicine-shipping industries.

“If successfully exploited, the actors could change the temperature and possibly cause physical impacts such as fire hazards, loss of inventory and changes to the service life of the system,” the agencies warn.

The warning comes after several waves of cyberattacks targeting industrial refrigeration units across the United Kingdom and Europe in recent weeks. Two separate waves of attacks allowed hackers to crank up the temperature on freezers and chilling units in at least a dozen countries, spoiling defrosted food and destroying produce. Some of the affected systems included remote-controlled refrigeration units made by Danish company Danfoss, which had stopped providing security updates to its customers’ freezers.

Hackers also targeted a blood bank in France, causing its refrigerated units to boost temperatures in its cold units containing donated blood supplies — but were stopped before the attack could compromise blood stores. The U.S. Department of Defense is investigating a spate of hacks targeting freezers run by the military, according to Reuters . The hacks were first reported by Signal and Silence .

The U.S. has not attributed the hacks to a particular group or government, but security researchers have broadly attributed the attacks to Iran ; U.S. officials also reportedly suspect Iran is the likely culprit .

CISA, the FBI, and the Departments of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation urged affected industries to remove remote control systems from the internet, change and strengthen passwords, apply patches where possible, and retire equipment that’s no longer supported by the vendor.

In a separate fact sheet , the departments said that hackers may attempt to “force units into continuous heating and defrost cycles, which can cause widespread inventory loss and equipment hazards.”

“Every organization that depends on refrigeration and monitoring systems should assume it could be a target,” said CISA’s acting cybersecurity chief Chris Butera.

articles.title: Fake Amazon invoice scam uses $988 iPad order as bait
articles.summary: A fake Amazon invoice charging $988.18 for an iPad lists the same customer support phone number three times to steer panicked victims into calling.
articles.body: You open your email and see an invoice from Amazon. It says you bought a new iPad for nearly $1,000. The order has supposedly shipped, and your payment has already gone through. There's even a customer support number to call if something looks wrong. Your first reaction might be to grab your phone and stop the charge. That's exactly what makes this fake Amazon invoice scam so dangerous. It uses a realistic-looking receipt and an expensive purchase to make you worry about your money. Then it offers what appears to be an easy solution. Matt, who lives in California, recently sent us one of these suspicious emails. He wanted to help others recognize the warning signs before someone falls for the same trick. After examining the message, we found several clues worth sharing. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money. Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com. DO NOT CLICK FAKE 'ACCOUNT RECOVERY' AMAZON EMAIL A fake Amazon invoice that looks surprisingly convincing Matt received the email on Oct. 28. Its subject line addressed him by name and claimed his order had already left the facility. Inside was a professionally formatted invoice featuring Amazon's familiar logo. The invoice listed an Apple iPad Air 11-inch (M4) with 256GB of storage and cellular connectivity. It showed a price of $973.19. Below that was an additional $14.99 charge labeled "Amazon Protect+ (Auto-Renew)." The grand total came to $988.18. The document also included an invoice number, shipping details and a delivery date. It even displayed Amazon's corporate address in Seattle. All those details helped create the appearance of a legitimate transaction. However, the email also included a phone number for canceling or modifying the order. That number appeared prominently near the top, again in the payment instructions and once more at the bottom. That's where the real concern begins. The message appears designed to make someone call before checking whether the purchase actually happened. Red flags in this fake Amazon invoice scam Let's look at the warning signs hiding in Matt's email. Some are obvious once you notice them. Others are more subtle and help explain why these scams can fool people. The sender's email address has nothing to do with Amazon This is the biggest giveaway. The email claimed to come from someone named Jack Campos. However, the actual sender address used Outlook.com with a different personal name embedded in the address. It had no apparent connection to Amazon. Amazon says its legitimate customer emails come from Amazon domains, including amazon.com. A personal Outlook account claiming to send an official Amazon invoice deserves immediate suspicion. Scammers can write almost anything in the sender's display name. That's why I always recommend checking the actual email address before trusting a message. The customer support phone number keeps appearing The invoice displayed the same customer support number in three separate locations. It appeared inside a shaded banner, within the payment instructions and again near the bottom. That's a significant warning sign because the email steers the recipient toward making a phone call. Rather than directing Matt to verify the purchase through his Amazon account, it emphasizes contacting the number printed on the invoice. That number should be treated as unverified and potentially controlled by scammers. We have not independently established who operates it. Amazon warns that fraudulent order confirmations often encourage customers to contact supposed support representatives. Those calls can turn into attempts to obtain payment information or gain access to an account. The invoice uses a nearly $1,000 charge to create anxiety Look at the amount: $988.18. That's enough money to get almost anyone's attention. If you saw that charge for a product you didn't buy, you'd probably want to fix it immediately. Scammers understand that reaction. They often choose expensive electronics because the potential financial loss feels serious. The detailed iPad description makes the transaction appear more believable. However, the amount on an email invoice proves nothing about your actual bank account. Until you verify the charge independently, treat it as an unsupported claim. The subject line contradicts the cancellation instructions Here's a detail I find especially revealing. The subject line claims the order has already left the facility. Yet the invoice says cancellations are accepted only before dispatch. So which is it? Has the package already shipped, or can the customer still cancel it? The conflicting language creates confusion while encouraging the recipient to seek help quickly. A concerned shopper may decide to call the listed number rather than spend time figuring out the inconsistency. The customer information looks generic The email addresses Matt by name in the subject line. However, the billing section identifies the customer as "Amazon Account Holder." The invoice also lacks a clear, personalized billing and shipping address. Instead, it provides broad fulfillment details and an estimated delivery date. Generic customer information alone doesn't prove fraud. Still, it raises questions when an email claims to document a completed purchase worth nearly $1,000. If the order were genuine, Matt should be able to locate its actual details inside his Amazon account. The payment language sounds strangely formal The invoice uses terms such as "Standard Account Allocation" and "active ledger." It also claims the authorization has been verified and automated order fulfillment is underway. Those phrases may sound official, but they provide little useful information about how the payment occurred. The email never gives Matt a reliable way to verify the transaction through his account. Scammers sometimes use corporate-sounding language to make a document seem authoritative. Don't assume unfamiliar financial terminology means the message came from a legitimate company. The mysterious auto-renewal charge raises another question Alongside the iPad, the invoice lists "Amazon Protect+ (Auto-Renew)" for $14.99. An unexpected recurring charge can create another reason for someone to contact support. Even if they aren't immediately concerned about the iPad, they might worry about paying for a subscription they never requested. The label alone doesn't establish whether the service exists or whether Matt was actually charged. However, any unfamiliar subscription on an unexpected invoice deserves verification through the company's official website. The invoice number looks official but proves nothing The document features an invoice identifier beginning with "AMZ" followed by additional letters and numbers. It looks technical enough to seem convincing. However, scammers can generate invoice numbers as easily as they can copy a company logo. An unfamiliar invoice identifier should never replace independent verification. Check Amazon's Your Orders section for a matching purchase instead. The dates and shipping details deserve a closer look The invoice shows October 28, 2026, as both the order date and estimated delivery date. It also claims that fulfillment has already moved forward. Same-day delivery can happen with legitimate Amazon orders, so that detail alone doesn't establish fraud. Still, the message offers no independently verifiable tracking information. It relies on its own claims about shipment and delivery. The document also lists zero estimated sales tax on the nearly $1,000 transaction. That may have a legitimate explanation depending on the circumstances. However, it adds another detail worth comparing with a real order record. The Amazon logo and Seattle address are meant to build trust Here's one of the more interesting details. The invoice includes the Amazon logo and lists Amazon.com Services LLC at 410 Terry Avenue North in Seattle, Washington. That address corresponds to an actual Amazon corporate location. This helps explain why the invoice can look credible. Scammers don't have to invent every detail. They can copy real company information and place it inside a fraudulent document. A legitimate address on a receipt doesn't authenticate the sender. The same goes for company logos and polished formatting. IDENTITY THIEVES DON’T NEED YOUR PASSWORD ANYMORE; HERE ARE 6 NEW ACCOUNT TAKEOVER THREATS What happens if you call the number on a fake Amazon invoice? The likely goal of this type of scam is to move you from an email conversation to a phone call. Once someone calls, a person posing as customer support may offer to cancel the purchase or reverse the charge. To complete that supposed refund, they might request payment details or account verification information. Some scammers also ask victims to install remote-access software. They may claim the installation is necessary to resolve a billing problem. In reality, that software could give a stranger access to the person's computer. Amazon specifically warns that its representatives will never ask you to share a one-time password over the phone. The company also cautions customers against providing financial details or granting unexpected remote access. These are documented tactics in Amazon impersonation scams. We haven't established what would happen if someone called the particular number in Matt's email. The most important point is that receiving a fake invoice does not mean you've actually been charged. "Scammers that attempt to impersonate Amazon put consumers at risk," an Amazon spokesperson told CyberGuy. "We will continue to invest in protecting consumers and educating the public on scam avoidance. We encourage consumers to report suspected scams to us so that we can protect their accounts and refer bad actors to law enforcement to help keep consumers safe. Please visit our help pages to find additional information on how to identify scams and report them at amazon.com/ReportAScam." What to do when a fake Amazon invoice arrives If an unexpected Amazon invoice lands in your inbox, don't rush to cancel the order or call the number provided. A few simple checks can help you determine whether the purchase is real. And if you've already contacted the supposed support team, there are steps you can take to protect your information. 1. Check your Amazon orders directly Open the official Amazon app or type Amazon.com into your browser. Select Your Orders and look for the alleged purchase. Avoid using links or phone numbers in the suspicious email. Going directly to your account helps you determine whether the order actually exists. 2. Review your Amazon Message Center Sign in to your Amazon account and look for Your Messages or Message Center under your account options. Amazon says authentic customer emails appear there. When a suspicious message doesn't appear, that's another reason to question its legitimacy. 3. Examine the sender's actual email address Expand the sender details instead of trusting the name displayed in your inbox. Scammers can make an email appear to come from Amazon while sending it through a personal account. Be especially suspicious of unfamiliar domains or addresses that have no connection to the company. 4. Never call the number printed on a suspicious invoice A fake customer support number can connect you directly to a scammer. Instead, find customer service through Amazon's official app or website. Remember, the person who sent the questionable invoice also supplied that phone number. 5. Use Amazon's AI scam verification tool Amazon now lets U.S. customers use Alexa for Shopping on Amazon.com or in the Amazon Shopping app to check suspicious emails, texts and phone calls. Simply ask, "Is this email from Amazon?" and provide details about the message. The tool checks the information against Amazon's records to determine whether the communication came from the company. If it can't verify the message, it will let you know. You can also forward suspicious emails to verify@amazon.com for verification. 6. Protect your account credentials Never share your Amazon password or one-time security codes with someone who contacts you unexpectedly. Consider setting up a passkey or enabling two-step verification for additional protection. These safeguards can make unauthorized account access more difficult, even when someone obtains your password. 7. Use strong antivirus software Strong antivirus protection can help detect malicious links, unsafe websites and harmful downloads that scammers may use to steal information. Choose reputable security software with real-time protection and keep it updated. While antivirus software cannot prevent someone from being tricked over the phone, it adds protection against other threats that often accompany scams. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com. 8. Check your financial accounts Review your bank and credit card transactions through their official apps or websites. Look for unfamiliar purchases or charges that don't match your records. Contact your financial institution immediately if you discover unauthorized activity. You can also enable transaction alerts to help catch suspicious charges sooner. 9. Consider a personal data removal service Scammers may use personal information found on data broker websites to make fraudulent emails more convincing. A personal data removal service can help remove your name, address, phone number and other details from covered people-search sites. Although these services cannot prevent every scam email, reducing your online exposure can make it harder for criminals to research and target you. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com 10. Consider an identity theft protection service Identity theft protection services can help monitor certain types of suspicious activity involving your personal information. Depending on the plan, you may receive alerts about unfamiliar credit activity or signs of identity misuse. Some services also offer professional restoration assistance if your identity becomes compromised. These protections can provide valuable support when criminals obtain sensitive information, although no service can detect every type of fraud. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com. 11. Report the suspicious email Visit Amazon's official scam reporting page to report the message. You can also report attempted fraud to the Federal Trade Commission at reportfraud.ftc.gov/. Amazon recommends that people without an Amazon account forward suspicious communications as an attachment to reportascam@amazon.com. Reporting these attempts helps companies and authorities identify fraudulent activity. For additional protection, we've also covered how Amazon alerts customers about impersonation scams and the precautions the company recommends. What to do if you already called the fake support number Already called the number on a suspicious Amazon invoice? Your next steps depend on what information you shared and whether you gave anyone access to your device. Here's how to protect yourself. The sooner you act, the better your chances of preventing additional damage. Even a short conversation with a scammer deserves attention if you shared personal information or allowed access to your device. Kurt's key takeaways I appreciate Matt taking the time to share this email with us. It's a good reminder of how much effort scammers put into making fraudulent communications look credible. What caught my attention was the combination of a detailed invoice and that repeatedly displayed phone number. The message creates concern about a large purchase, then conveniently offers a way to fix it. That's where people can get pulled into a scam before they realize what's happening. And here's something worth remembering: You don't have to spot every strange detail on an invoice to protect yourself. You only need to recognize that an unexpected charge deserves independent verification. The lesson I take from Matt's experience is simple. Don't let a scary email decide whom you call or how quickly you act. Check your account through an official channel before you give anyone access to your money or personal information. I'm glad Matt reached out because sharing these examples gives more people a chance to recognize the warning signs. articles.title: LIV golf to shutter league, lawyer says in bankruptcy hearing
articles.summary: LIV Golf is shuttering after five years that fractured the sport’s landscape, announcing Thursday in bankruptcy court it plans to wind down operations instead of launching a new version because it didn’t have enough support.
articles.body:
TRENTON, N.J. (AP) — LIV Golf is shuttering after five years that fractured the sport’s landscape, announcing Thursday in bankruptcy court it plans to wind down operations instead of launching a new version because it didn’t have enough support.

“The debtors are not currently proceeding with the LIV 2.0 plan,” attorney Matthew Williams of Gibson Dunn said in a hearing in New Jersey. “Instead, the debtors are toggling to a value-maximizing wind-down in their business.”

LIV Golf, which launched in June 2022 by offering nine-figure signing bonuses to lure top names away from the PGA Tour, lost Saudi Arabia funding in April after spending more than $5 billion.

It filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Sept. 8 and thought it had a lifeline in BC Partners Credit, which pledged a $300 million investment to pivot to a more financially sustainable “LIV 2.0.” But players like Jon Rahm and Sergio Garcia, Tyrrell Hatton and Louis Oosthuizen, weren’t interested.

“BC Partners Credit supported a transaction that aligned the interests of players and investors, offering a credible path toward building a sustainable future for LIV Golf,” BC Partners said in a statement. “While there was great support for the league, we are disappointed that mutually acceptable terms could not be reached among the various stakeholders.”

Instead of planning for a new version for 2027, LIV enters a liquidation phase.

Rahm already agreed to forfeit all claims against LIV — said to be worth some $100 million — to get out of his contract. He is back to playing the European tour, with hopes there will be a path back to the PGA Tour. The tour currently has a one-year ban dating to players’ last LIV appearance.

LIV Golf paid $15.6 million to retain seven of its executives , including $6.375 million to CEO Scott O’Neil, in the months between the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia and LIV filing for bankruptcy. Those payments are not unusual for a company trying to emerge from bankruptcy. The question now is whether those payments can be voided since LIV isn’t going forward.

LIV suffered two big setbacks, before and after filing for bankruptcy.

The Asian Tour, which received financial support from LIV for an International Series, decided in July to renew an alliance with the PGA Tour and the commercially known DP World Tour in Europe.

Then, European tour CEO Guy Kinnings last month said anyone signing up for LIV 2.0 need not apply for membership on the European tour, which put European players at risk of having no part in the Ryder Cup.

Kinnings said in an interview with The Scotsman newspaper earlier this week, “But we also have to protect the tour against an entity who spent, so we are told, over $7 billion, with one of their aims being to ‘destroy the DP World Tour.’”

But the biggest setback was in April, two weeks after the Masters and two months after the start of the Iran war. PIF changed its investment strategy and said it would no longer pay for LIV Golf after the 2026 season.

LIV was originally run by Greg Norman, who tried unsuccessfully to start a world tour in 1994 only to have it quashed by Arnold Palmer and the PGA Tour. Norman had Saudi money at his disposal, and promoted LIV as “Golf, but louder” with its blaring music, 54-hole shotgun starts and $25 million in prize funds — individual and team — at each event.

But it had no broadcast deal the first year, meaning it had to cover production costs. It got the CW Network in 2023, and eventually got Fox Sports to sign on in 2025.

The year began with Brooks Koepka getting out of his LIV deal with one year remaining, and the PGA Tour created a path — with financial penalties — to return. Patrick Reed chose not to extend his deal and now is poised to return to the PGA Tour next year through his performance in Europe.

Rahm had said on Tuesday he would be willing to pay the same price as Koepka, though it was unlikely that same deal would be offered.

LIV 2.0 was pushing player equity and prize money that was more than half the $20 million purses for individuals when it began in 2022. LIV’s final event was in August in Indianapolis, won by Michael La Sasso. He failed to get through the second stage of European tour Q-school last week.

articles.title: Centcom launches podcast amid Iran war backlash
articles.summary: As the Trump administration’s deeply unpopular war in Iran stretches into its ninth month, U.S. Central Command (Centcom) has launched an official podcast that kicked off Thursday with its top commander bantering about stealing french fries from his colleague and only briefly referring to the ongoing conflict. Titled “Inside Centcom,” the inaugural episode came in…
articles.body:
As the Trump administration’s deeply unpopular war in Iran stretches into its ninth month, U.S. Central Command (Centcom) has launched an official podcast that kicked off Thursday with its top commander bantering about stealing french fries from his colleague and only briefly referring to the ongoing conflict.

Titled “Inside Centcom,” the inaugural episode came in at just under 12 minutes and featured the command’s head Adm. Brad Cooper and Fleet Master Chief Lateef Compton, Centcom’s senior enlisted leader.

Compton said the podcast, released Thursday, was meant to offer insights into how the command operates and to give the American people “an opportunity to get to know the incredible people that make up our team.”

“It’s been a busy year,” Compton said at the top of the episode, questioning Cooper about his personal fitness routine, what he eats for lunch, his time as a junior officer and his favorite NFL team, among other light topics.

Compton and Cooper’s banter steered clear of much mention of the Iran war, referring once to its official name, Operation Epic Fury. The conflict, which began on Feb. 28, has morphed into a quagmire for the administration — roiling global markets, sending fuel costs soaring and adding to crippling GOP losses in the midterm elections this week.

Both President Trump and Vice President Vance have blamed Republicans’ loss of the House and Senate on the war.

“For sure, no one could have imagined the trajectory of events that we would be on, but through it, everyone has been doing a fantastic job,” Cooper said during the podcast.

At one point, Compton joked with Cooper about his love of french fries.

“You are the original fry guy. You like french fries. Most people don’t notice, but I did notice when we stationed together years ago, my lunch would come, and I always had french fries,” Compton said. “You would see my french fries coming on my plate. You’d at least take one or two, and they would tell me … I don’t think you ever knew that I knew you took my french fries. So, is that your favorite food, french fries?”

Cooper responded: “You should let the world know. For years, I’ve been eating your french fries. The secret is now out. But yeah, I never met a french fry I didn’t like, and thus the need to exercise frequently to balance that out.”

articles.title: Hegseth amid impeachment threats: ‘Didn’t work against’ Trump, ‘won’t work with me’
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth shot back Thursday against threats of impeachment. In a video posted Thursday afternoon on the social platform X, Hegseth said that “a disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly,” referencing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.). “Just like they tried against…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth shot back Thursday against threats of impeachment.

In a video posted Thursday afternoon on the social platform X, Hegseth said that “a disgruntled, defeated congressman, along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly,” referencing Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.).

“Just like they tried against President Trump twice. You see, their policies don’t work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents. It’s all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me. You can rest assured of that,” Hegseth added.

On Thursday morning, Massie said his push to impeach the Defense secretary is “a much gentler version” of what could happen when Democrats, who won back the House and Senate this week, take control of Congress.

The Kentucky Republican said he planned to call a vote to impeach Hegseth, according to CNN . He also said in a post Wednesday on X that “there is one contingency in which I won’t reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns.”

Massie then posted Thursday on X, “My Hegseth impeachment resolution is a much gentler version of what’s coming when Dem’s control Congress. They’ll have hearings & trials.”

Multiple Democrats have signaled pushing Hegseth out of his role in the wake of their blowout victories in Congress.

“Why is Pete Hegseth still around?” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.), who is widely considered to be the next Speaker of the House, said in a post Thursday on X.

President Trump has supported Hegseth amid questions over his future.

“Pete Hegseth has done a fantastic job,” Trump told reporters Thursday in the Oval Office when asked about possible staffing changes in the Pentagon.

articles.title: The midterms proved once and for all that X is not real life
articles.summary: The Verge is about technology and how it makes us feel. Founded in 2011, we offer our audience everything from breaking news to reviews to award-winning features and investigations, on our site, in video, and in podcasts.
articles.body: A week before the midterm elections, Vice President JD Vance hosted a town hall in Texas with Fox News host Jesse Watters. It was a friendly event with a friendly audience in what should have been a friendly state, and maybe that’s why Vance couldn’t help himself. When a college student earnestly asked how the right expected young people like her to settle down and have kids, given the ever-growing cost of living, Vance replied with a quip about Jon Husted’s ass. The student, Kate White, introduced herself as the vice president of the Texas Christian University chapter of Turning Point USA, the conservative group started by Donald Trump ally Charlie Kirk. She was offering Vance an opportunity to explain how MAGA could work for young people, and he turned it into a joke. Vance did eventually answer the question, saying Republicans don’t pay enough attention to the issue of affordability and blaming rising housing costs on institutional investors and the “20 million illegal aliens” supposedly living in the United States. But the order of operations revealed the fatal flaw of Republicans’ 2026 strategy: Everything is a gag to them, and they’re way too online. For the past decade, Republicans have adhered to Steve Bannon’s maxim that politics is downstream from culture. This fixation with liberals’ alleged capture of elite institutions has animated the right’s war against Big Tech and in particular social media platforms — which the right claims actively silenced conservative voices — and its crusade against diversity, equity, and inclusion. With his purchase of X, Elon Musk finally succeeded in building a conservative platform where right-wing voices not only had real influence but also a direct line to those in power. More recently, some people have claimed that Musk’s X is the only social media that really represents the people, unlike platforms like Bluesky, which have more left-leaning user bases. Cocooned in their online echo chamber, MAGA figureheads convinced themselves the public was on their side, even when polling suggested otherwise. They ignored their base’s valid concerns about affordability and served them nonsensical memes instead. And they failed spectacularly in the realm where it actually mattered: politics. X, we can now declare once and for all, is not real life. Republicans not only lost historically red states like Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina, but barely managed to win Florida. The Senate race in Mississippi, of all places, is still too close to call. Vance, especially, is a creature of X, where his following list includes such illustrious accounts as Raw Egg Nationalist, Bronze Age Pervert, Howling Mutant, and Captive Dreamer. But White House aides, department employees, and Hill staffers are stewing in the same ecosystem. Writer John Ganz has termed this phenomenon “groyperfication,” after followers of influencer Nick Fuentes, who call themselves groypers. This is a useful shorthand, though Fuentes’ fans are mostly too NEET-pilled to land jobs on the Hill. American Moment, a boot camp for young conservative up-and-comers, reportedly screens out groypers. There’s a real need for such protective measures. Kingsley Wilson, the hard-right press secretary for the Department of War (or per its legal name, Defense), has posted antisemitic conspiracy theories about Leo Frank, a Jewish man who was lynched in Georgia 1915 for allegedly raping a teenage girl. (Historians largely believe Frank was innocent.) The Department of Homeland Security regularly posts fascist fancams and wink-wink references to white supremacist memes. Republicans saw their 2024 victory as a mandate. Having clawed the White House and Congress back from Democrats, they assumed the public was on board with MAGA’s cultural project when in fact people were largely mad about the price of eggs. And with two years of dominance under their belt, they decided to go even harder on culture, not realizing — or maybe just not caring — that people are still mad about gas prices and groceries. In the run-up to the midterms, the Department of Education was posting about “Malfoid” — a gender-swapped version of Draco Malfoy from Harry Potter that far-right influencers claimed would save Western literature from the scourge of wokeness. The Department of Homeland Security was bragging about record lows in legal immigration, which outside white nationalist circles is typically not considered a negative thing. Pseudonymous shitposters like Howling Mutant were posting memes comparing themselves to noted child murderer Anakin Skywalker, the new avatar for the online right. Musk, a Republican megadonor, got in on the fun, as did Katie Miller, wife of ultranationalist White House adviser Stephen Miller, who dressed up as Anakin’s wife Padmé Amidala for Halloween. (Katie Miller’s last government role was advising Elon Musk’s failed Department of Government Efficiency; now she devotes her time to throwing lavish parties and hosting a podcast no one listens to.) Most of the American public isn’t on X, but the conversations conservatives have there do bleed out into the mainstream — often with disastrous results. Bo French, the Republican candidate for Texas railroad commissioner, lost his election by a huge margin after posting anti-Indian memes on X. (Asian American voters, including Indian Americans, moved to the left in Texas elections down the ballot.) Musk did his part to drive turnout, spending nearly half a billion dollars on Republican candidates and PACs. But even Musk’s money failed to make up for voters’ dissatisfaction with Republicans’ performance, perhaps because the ads he funded focused largely on culture war issues that were out of step with voters’ concerns about the cost of living. [Media: And Miller, it turns out, didn’t even vote, telling CBS News she feared doing so would put her safety at risk, since Virginia law makes voters’ home addresses public. (The Millers, like other members of the Trump administration, live on a military installation with tight security; it’s unlikely intruders would be able to get to their home.) Republican myopia may have contributed to their poor performance across the board, including with groups that were touted as their new base. One poll found that a majority of young men of all races — including young white men — voted for Democrats in the midterms. In a long postmortem on X — reportedly posted without input or permission from White House officials — Vance said he asked “the smartest data guy” he knows for insight on the electorate ahead of the midterms. Vance claims several pollsters told him that voters’ main concerns were the war against Iran, the cost of living, and America’s relationship to Israel. So why didn’t Republicans listen? The answer lies in the algorithmic nature of social media, X especially. If you interact with even one post about a relatively niche topic — say, genderbent Harry Potter fanfiction — the algorithm will feed you post after post after post about the same thing. Just like Trump spent the early years of his first term obsessing over Fox News, the single mainstream network that would reflect his biases back to him, MAGA is now all in on X. And if you’re the kind of person who spends a lot of time scrolling, you may even delude yourself into thinking the issue clogging up your feed is something people just can’t stop talking about.

articles.title: Salon is shutting down after 31 years
articles.summary: Salon.com is shutting down after launching 31 years ago as one of the first purely online news publishers.
articles.body: Salon launched 31 years ago as one of the first online-only news magazine outlets, and it announced today in an unsigned post that it’s ceasing publication. The company said that the “business realities of independent digital journalism have changed profoundly over the years,” and it decided that its publishing model is “no longer sustainable.” It didn’t go into detail about why, but many websites are grappling with “Google Zero” and the impact of AI tools. When reached for comment, Salon general manager Amanda Wolfe pointed The Verge to today’s announcement post. “Thirty-one years is a remarkable run, but what matters most is what happened during those years: the journalism, the ideas, the voices, the conversations and the community that grew around them,” Salon said in its post. “Salon helped demonstrate what digital journalism could be and could become. We hope that legacy will continue to matter long after today.” On Bluesky, Salon chief content officer Erin Keane says that the editorial archive will “stay live for now.” Current Salon owner Find.co acquired Salon in 2023 and describes itself as a “Performance Marketing Ecosystem transforming crypto marketing with performance and precision.”

articles.title: Wisconsin reports first measles death since 1990
articles.summary: Wisconsin reported Thursday that an infant died in connection to the ongoing measles outbreak — the state’s first measles-related death in more than 30 years. The state’s Division of Public Health (DPH) with the Department of Health Services said in a statement that the coroner had listed the immediate cause of death as measles. “It…
articles.body:
Wisconsin reported Thursday that an infant died in connection to the ongoing measles outbreak — the state’s first measles-related death in more than 30 years.

The state’s Division of Public Health (DPH) with the Department of Health Services said in a statement that the coroner had listed the immediate cause of death as measles.

“It is with a heavy heart we are reporting the first death of an infant connected with a measles outbreak in Wisconsin in many years. My heart is broken for the family,” Wisconsin’s Health Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement.

“Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease. Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family,” said Johnson.

As of Thursday, Wisconsin has confirmed 431 cases of measles and nine related hospitalizations.

Wisconsin now joins Pennsylvania and New York as states that have reported measles-associated deaths in 2026. Pennsylvania on Wednesday confirmed a sixth measles death , though CDC data is not yet reflecting the total reported by states.

Wisconsin ranks among the states with the lowest coverage of measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations. According to DPH, 79.8 percent of children had received one or more doses of the MMR vaccine by the time they were 24 months old.

The state is currently fourth in terms of absolute number of measles cases nationally, behind Pennsylvania, South Carolina and Utah.

Most of Wisconsin’s measles cases are concentrated in the state’s southwestern region. DPH data indicates there are counties in that region where fewer children aged 2 or younger are vaccinated against measles, with Vernon County reporting a coverage rate of 42.3 percent in 2025. Neighboring counties like Crawford, Richland and Monroe have MMR vaccination rates in the 60-percent range.

articles.title: MAHA leader open to working with Democrats who won’t fight RFK Jr.
articles.summary: A top leader in the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement said he is willing to work with Democrats if they share his vision, after Republicans were trounced out of power in Tuesday’s midterm elections. Tony Lyons, a key ally of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. who runs several MAHA political…
articles.body:
A top leader in the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) movement said he is willing to work with Democrats if they share his vision, after Republicans were trounced out of power in Tuesday’s midterm elections.

Tony Lyons, a key ally of Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. who runs several MAHA political committees, said Wednesday that the movement must work with anyone who shares its goals.

To move forward, “we partner with absolutely everyone who’s willing to partner with us — companies who will listen, politicians who will work with us from any party, activists, influencers, MAHA moms in every corner of the country,” Lyons said during a virtual call with supporters.

“There are good people across the political spectrum who want to be part of this, and we’re going to find every last one of them and fight with them,” Lyons added.

Lyons previously encouraged MAHA supporters to only back Republicans to shore up Kennedy’s alliance with President Trump and MAGA. Lyons’s PACs endorsed and supported only Republicans in the run-up to the elections.

MAHA helped give Trump an important ally in Kennedy, a longtime Democrat before he endorsed Trump and joined his administration. That gave Republicans access to a new group of voters with the hope they would turn out for the GOP again during the midterms.

But there was tension from the start. MAHA principles, especially those that push for clean water and food at the expense of pesticides and farm profits, are often at odds with the Republican Party’s historically pro-business agenda.

Republican lawmakers have also opposed efforts to regulate ultra-processed food and ban pesticides and food dyes, siding with corporate efforts to lobby the White House to scale back those efforts.

MAHA supporters, who have historically been a loose collection of groups without a set political party, repeatedly said they felt betrayed by Republicans and the Trump administration.

On Tuesday, major MAHA-aligned Republican politicians in Iowa, Texas and Kansas lost, dealing a major blow to Kennedy and his allies in the movement.

The most significant defeat for Kennedy and the vaccine-skeptic wing of the MAHA movement came when Iowa GOP gubernatorial candidate Zach Lahn lost in a landslide to Democrat Rob Sand.

Kennedy and MAHA groups invested significant time and money promoting Lahn, who vowed to ban COVID-19 vaccines, end school vaccine mandates, clean Iowa’s water and regulate chemicals if elected.

Some Democrats, including Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (N.Y.) and Michigan’s Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, ran on a “Building a Healthier America” policy agenda that addressed major MAHA concerns like pesticide company accountability, removing toxic chemicals from food and the water supply, and breaking up “Big Ag” monopolies.

Lyons previously dismissed those attempts.

“She is not our ally,” Lyons said of Ocasio-Cortez in September. “She is just another double-talking politician, who is preparing to run for president on a platform of lies, slogans and propaganda.”

On Wednesday following the GOP’s midterm carnage, Lyons did not dismiss those outreach efforts outright.

He challenged Democrats to follow through on their words with actions and to work with Kennedy.

“They have to get out of this idea that Bobby Kennedy is somehow bad, that their job is to somehow get rid of him instead of address the points that he brought up,” Lyons said. “If they believe the things that they’ve been saying in the last month. It felt disingenuous, but I’m open … to the possibility that they mean it.”

articles.title: Lawsuit claims AI on Google’s school Chromebook helped plan teen’s near-suicide
articles.summary: Parents are suing technology giant Google, alleging the AI Gemini chatbot offered on school Chromebooks helped a young teen plan her near-suicide and funeral. The lawsuit, filed in California Superior Court on Wednesday, claims a 13-year-old girl, dubbed Emma, chatted with Gemini over the course of several months, prompting a “severe psychological crisis.” The complaint…
articles.body:
Parents are suing technology giant Google, alleging the AI Gemini chatbot offered on school Chromebooks helped a young teen plan her near-suicide and funeral.

The lawsuit , filed in California Superior Court on Wednesday, claims a 13-year-old girl, dubbed Emma, chatted with Gemini over the course of several months, prompting a “severe psychological crisis.” The complaint alleges Google’s top executives knew Gemini was dangerous and released it anyway.

“As her Gemini chats grew more frequent… Emma became convinced that she was afflicted by a battery of major psychological disorders and that suicide was her only way out,” the EdTech Law Center, representing Emma and her parents, wrote in a press release.

Lawyers said she exchanged “thousands of messages” with Gemini and after three months, asked the chatbot about various ways to commit suicide. The chatbot allegedly told Emma how to hide her mental health and self-harm from people around her and helped her play a funeral.

A former school counsel who received alerts from the school’s third-party monitoring software told Emma’s parents, who logged into her account and intervened.

José Castañeda, a spokesperson for Google, said the company is reviewing the claims and takes the claims “very seriously.”

“We’ve worked extensively with medical professionals and academic experts to build features that help young people find critical support and trusted resources when they need it,” Castañeda said.

“Our systems aim to prevent users from engaging in harmful conversations, and when people’s queries indicate they may be experiencing a crisis, we show hotline information directly in Search to connect them with real-world support,” he added.

According to Google, the company has worked on its crisis detection system for decades, building certain protections for users in crisis. It also has SafeSearch, a filter for explicit content, which is turned on for all education users under 18.

Emma’s lawyers claim she did not seek out Gemini, but “it just showed up in Google search one day.”

The suit is the latest in hundreds of cases filed against social media and AI platforms over alleged harms to young users.

Emma is bringing claims for detective design, failure to warn, negligence, fraudulent concealment and infliction of emotional concealment.

“What happened to Emma is an outrage. Google has no right to use its stranglehold on public schools to force its dangerous Gemini chatbot on a captive audience of millions of kids,” said Julie Liddell, founder of the EdTech Law Center.

Earlier this week, Google faced heavy pushback for announcing students using their software in the classroom will not be permitted to access their search engine unless the school system approves AI use.

This came after Google announced in August it turned on its Gemini chatbot for many K-12 students using Google classroom. Chris Phillips, vice president for education at Google, told The New York Times that “Search and AI are “deeply integrated.”

Several lawmakers called out Google’s move this week, arguing it reflected the company’s monopoly in the online search sector.

Responding to the backlash, Google posted a clarification on X, stating the move was to give “schools more choice, not less.”

By default, Gemini, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off, but schools “can choose to turn on one, two, or all of the services.

“We know there’s concern about students using AI to shortcut schoolwork, and schools have told us they want control,” the company said. “That’s exactly why we are making these changes today to address the feedback we’ve heard from educators in recent months. And we’ll continue to engage deeply with educators to ensure we are giving schools more choice, more controls, and improved Search for learning.”

articles.title: Top GOP House lawmakers want Nvidia’s Jensen Huang to come to Congress
articles.summary: House Select Committee on China Chair John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Fl.) and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chair Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent a letter to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang following reports he sent intelligence to China. The GOP lawmakers requested Huang appear in a joint, closed-door briefing on…
articles.body:
House Select Committee on China Chair John Moolenaar (R-Mich.), House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast (R-Fl.) and House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence Chair Rick Crawford (R-Ark.) sent a letter to Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang following reports he sent intelligence to China.

The GOP lawmakers requested Huang appear in a joint, closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 to address concerns regarding “NVIDIA’s security protocols against foreign adversary espionage and your interactions with…Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.”

The New York Times published a report in October alleging American spy agencies last year discovered Alice Huang, an executive at the Singapore-based data center Megaspeed, funneled information to Beijing while developing a “close relationship” with Trump-ally Jensen Huang.

Nvidia previously told The Hill that Megaspeed was a regional customer and the claims were debunked last year.

President Trump was briefed on the matter but was reportedly hesitant to interfere with Nvidia’s chip sales and the U.S.’s trading relationship with China, per The Times.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the lawmakers wrote in a statement, adding that it is “vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”

The Nvidia chief has until Nov. 11 to provide alternative availability if he cannot attend the mid-Nov. hearing.

Huang has navigated a trade war between the U.S. and China over the past year and a half that saw restrictions on the most advanced tech infrastructure sales to Beijing. Though exceptions were made for Nvidia, particularly, to sell older AI chips to China in 2025.

An Nvidia spokesperson told The Hill, that “meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen [Huang] talks with thousands of customer executives every year.”

“Our regional cloud customers receive ordinary business information—not sensitive NVIDIA trade secrets—and zero information relevant to national security.”

“We’re confident that if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know,” the spokesperson expressed, adding that the regional cloud customers “receive ordinary business information” that is “not sensitive Nvidia trade secrets.”

In another statement from Oct. 29, an Nvidia spokesperson asserted that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected.”

articles.title: National Guard to use boats, Humvees in expanded DC presence
articles.summary: The National Guard will begin using boats, up to 60 marked police cars, and military tactical vehicles in Washington, D.C., after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth authorized the move late last month, a Pentagon official confirmed to The Hill on Thursday. Hegseth authorized the changes in an Oct. 29 memo first reported by Politico, though it…
articles.body:
The National Guard will begin using boats, up to 60 marked police cars, and military tactical vehicles in Washington, D.C., after Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth authorized the move late last month, a Pentagon official confirmed to The Hill on Thursday.

Hegseth authorized the changes in an Oct. 29 memo first reported by Politico , though it is unclear what prompted the action that is sure to escalate the National Guard’s presence in the nation’s capital – and in some cases make it difficult to discern between military members and local police.

The guidance “authorizes the use of up to 60 marked patrol cars, military tactical vehicles, up to 20 light towers and generators, and D.C. National Guard maritime boat assets in support of federal and local law enforcement operations,” the official said, adding that the capabilities would be in support of the White House’s Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful mission.

They did not say which military vehicles would be used, though Politico reported the memo as specifying Humvees and light medium tactical vehicles, equipment that is typically used on the battlefield.

Troops are not allowed to pursue suspects or make arrests using the military vehicles, which are to be in place through the end of the year, according to the outlet.

The added boats, meanwhile, will offer “perimeter security” for police pursuing suspected gang leaders and drug traffickers in the southeast area of the city known as Anacostia. The vessels will not be used to carry out surveillance on U.S. citizens, and Hegseth stipulates that federal officers “must always be on board” Guard vessels “to help arrest a criminal suspect” should they attempt to escape by jumping into the water, according to the memo, as reported by Politico.

The National Guard Bureau referred a request for comment to the Pentagon.

Just under 3,100 National Guard troops are in D.C. as part of a deployment since late last summer, when the federal government ⁠temporarily took ​over the city’s law ​enforcement through ‌presidential executive order. The number of guardsmen has fluctuated in the course of a year, swelling to roughly 5,000 ahead of the Fourth of July festivities.

Critics say the Guard’s presence is not only expensive — with the deployment projected to cost roughly $2.1 billion through the end of President Trump’s second term — but also unnecessary and ineffective at curbing violent crimes. Guardsmen can’t make arrests and largely patrol neighborhoods and tourist centers that typically have lower crime rates.

City officials, Democrats and civil liberty advocates also have called the mission an infringement on Americans’ civil liberties and lacking a clear strategy.

The ineffectiveness at curbing violent crime argument has been backed up by several studies, including one from the Niskanen Center in May . The policy think tank found that the guard’s presence helped drive down opportunistic property crime but found it was not the correct tool for violent offenses and comes at a far higher cost than traditional police law enforcement.

Then in July the Center for American Progress (CAP), a liberal think tank, released a report suggesting the National Guard deployments failed to reduce violent crime, findings Trump lashed out at .

More recently, the libertarian Cato Institute last month found that while robberies and theft fell in Washington since the Guard was first deployed, it didn’t shift the needle on homicides, and assaults with dangerous weapons actually went up.

Guard troops, a common sight as they conduct patrols in small groups throughout the city, are expected to remain in Washington through Inauguration Day 2029.

articles.title: Hegseth in ‘trouble’ as Trump faces music on Iran war, midterms
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s future leading the Pentagon looks increasingly uncertain as his critics within the administration blame him for helping push President Trump into a war that contributed to massive midterm losses Tuesday. Two sources familiar with the discussion said the president is asking allies about Hegseth’s standing. One of those sources said the…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s future leading the Pentagon looks increasingly uncertain as his critics within the administration blame him for helping push President Trump into a war that contributed to massive midterm losses Tuesday.

Two sources familiar with the discussion said the president is asking allies about Hegseth’s standing. One of those sources said the Defense chief is in “a lot of trouble,” while the other said it wasn’t clear how much his position was in jeopardy. Both spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive matters.

At the same time, the administration is reviewing plans to resume military operations against Iran, one of the two sources said.

Trump has stood by Hegseth in public and told reporters Thursday his mind wasn’t made up on the future of the war.

“I would rather not destroy the rest of the country, if possible, but maybe I will have to,” Trump told reporters Thursday at the White House. “You will know soon enough.”

A senior Pentagon official told The Hill on Thursday that the idea of Hegseth being replaced is not “practical,” pointing to the potential difficulty of finding a replacement who could be confirmed by the Senate during the lame-duck — and before Democrats take control of the upper chamber.

“He is not terribly worried about being replaced,” the senior Pentagon official said.

The Defense secretary’s standing in Congress has been on a downturn among both Democrats and Republicans, who have demanded more transparency from the Pentagon regarding the Iran war and defense spending plans.

A Republican congressional official said Hegseth’s position had become “completely untenable” from a Capitol Hill standpoint.

“Keeping him in would require the White House to spend all of their political capital defending him from impeachment proceedings and drag the president into endless news cycles about the war, firing generals, Signalgate and more,” this official told The Hill on Thursday.

Hegseth and allied social media accounts made a concerted effort to push back Thursday.

In a video recorded in front of the Pentagon, Hegseth slammed Rep. Thomas Massie’s (R-Ky.) impeachment salvo and pushed once again for Congress to greenlight the $350 billion defense reconciliation package.

“This is not about me, but of course the other side. In case you’ve noticed, they’re obsessed. A disgruntled, defeated congressman , along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly, just like they tried against President Trump twice,” Hegseth said in the video posted Thursday.

“You see, their policies don’t work, so their obsession with political theater disguised as power drives them to try to destroy their opponents,” he said. “It’s all about the politics of personal destruction. Didn’t work against President Trump, and it won’t work with me.”

The Pentagon press team started making social media posts in support of the Defense secretary Thursday, writing, “Stand. Fight. Defend the Republic.”

The Pentagon did not respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The White House posted an 80-second video to the social platform X touting Hegseth’s tenure at the Pentagon.

“We are not defenders anymore. We are warriors,” the Pentagon chief said in that video.

The speculation surrounding Hegseth’s future follows Vice President Vance’s move to blame the GOP’s midterm defeats on the Iran war, of which he’s been a vocal opponent within the administration.

“When you have the sitting VP say Iran is a mistake, the support for the conflict and Hegseth by extension is going to evaporate,” one defense-world source said Thursday.

But a senior administration official said anyone “looking to point fingers should start looking for another scapegoat,” as the Pentagon and the White House have made their positions on Hegseth “crystal clear.”

“They are coming out swinging in support of Hegseth, and that should tell you everything you need to know,” the official said.

“Suggesting he’s looking for an exit or preparing to step aside is delusional thinking and misreading the situation. He’s not going anywhere,” the official added. “He’s going to remain focused on his mission, he won’t be distracted by the noise and he’s not going to let the pressure dictate his future.”

Inside the Pentagon, questions are swirling about how long Hegseth lasts even if he is not impeached, The Hill has reported.

Those who have broken with Hegseth, including a former Army National Guard major, argued the former Fox News co-host shouldn’t have overseen the Pentagon in the first place.

“For almost two years now, we’ve had a cross between a court jester and a personal trainer running the Pentagon, and it’s done real damage to the President and to Republicans. If Hegseth were truly loyal to President Trump, he would have stepped aside long ago — or better yet, never taken a job he wasn’t qualified for,” said John Ullyot, former Pentagon spokesperson under Hegseth and author of the new book “ The President Deserves Better .”

Hegseth is seen as one of the chief Iran war backers in the administration — something Trump has publicly recognized.

“Pete, I think you were the first one to speak up, and you said let’s do it because you can’t let them have a nuclear weapon,” Trump said in late March.

The pressure on Hegseth will go up next week as Massie, a vocal Iran war critic, plans to reintroduce eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth, an effort that has House Democrats lining up behind it.

Massie, who lost his reelection to Hegseth-backed former Navy SEAL Ed Gallrein, said the only thing that could stop him is Hegseth resigning on his own accord.

Mark Lucas, a Hegseth ally, said that Democrats are using Massie and Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.) to drive the impeachment push and that his organization Veteran Action will hold any Republican accountable who supports the effort.

“And if you ever hope to have a political future in the Republican Party, you better vote that resolution down. It’s bigger than Pete Hegseth. It’s bigger than Donald Trump,” Lucas said during his appearance on Steve Bannon’s “War Room” show.

CBS News reported Wednesday that Trump was considering replacing Hegseth with Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R), who is term-limited and leaving office in January. However, one source said DeSantis is not interested in the role.

Trump has maintained that he has no plans to remove Hegseth from his role but noted in a phone interview with ABC News on Thursday that it would be easier to confirm a new Defense secretary while Republicans still have their majorities before next year.

The president also said Wednesday that Hegseth would be a “very popular” Tennessee senator if he filled Sen. Marsha Blackburn’s (R) seat.

Hegseth is interested in the open Tennessee Senate seat , which expires in 2031, and has been campaigning behind the scenes for the post, The Hill previously reported . Blackburn has shown no signs of supporting the move.

“I think he’s doing a very good job, and I actually think he’d be very popular if he did that. But I haven’t heard that at all,” the president told reporters Wednesday.

When pressed again on potential staffing changes involving Hegseth, the president said Thursday his Defense secretary “has done a fantastic job.”

“We had more generals than we did in World War II. We had so many generals. Everybody was a four-star general. I never saw anything like it, and many of those people were woke,” he continued. “I don’t like a woke general, so he probably has opposition. I think he’s doing a fantastic job.”

Hegseth was seen walking into the West Wing earlier Thursday.

Massie also encouraged the president to replace Hegseth during the lame-duck period.

However, with only a few weeks of floor time and many competing priorities, replacing a defense secretary in the middle of a war may not be a top GOP priority.

Even if Trump did attempt a switch, a number of departing Republican senators who have locked horns with Trump, including Republican Sens. John Cornyn (Texas), Bill Cassidy (La.), and Mitch McConnell (Ky.), may not be generous with their confirmation votes.

On the Senate side, Democrats are quietly floating the defense secretary’s removal following the midterms, using Hegseth as leverage in defense spending talks with the administration, The Hill previously reported . And they could have some GOP support.

Hegseth’s message to service members on Thursday was to remain focused on the mission.

“To the troops, don’t blink, ignore the noise, never hesitate,” he said. “You see, all this is politics. You do real things, so stay the course.”

The negotiations with the Times Company have included the potential for Letterboxd’s co-founders to stay in charge but report to a Times Company executive. articles.title: Meta, TikTok, Google sue California over child online safety restrictions
articles.summary: Meta, TikTok and Google filed separate lawsuits against California over a new law seeking to tighten restrictions on child social media usage, arguing the legislation violates the companies’ First Amendment rights. California’s bipartisan “Digital Age Assurance Act,” which goes into effect Jan. 1, bans social media platforms in the Sunshine State from providing “an addictive…
articles.body:
Meta, TikTok and Google filed separate lawsuits against California over a new law seeking to tighten restrictions on child social media usage, arguing the legislation violates the companies’ First Amendment rights.

California’s bipartisan “ Digital Age Assurance Act ,” which goes into effect Jan. 1, bans social media platforms in the Sunshine State from providing “an addictive feed” to users under the age of 16. It also requires these companies “implement reasonable measures” to prevent minors from accessing such features.

The three companies argued the bill violates both the First Amendment and the federal Communications Decency Act, which protects online platforms from being sued over third party content. However, the law, established in 1996, went into effect as social media was in its early infancy.

A spokesperson for California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) said the office was reviewing the filings.

“Our office is committed to defending California’s commonsense laws to protect kids online,” the spokesperson said.

In Meta’s lawsuit , attorneys described the California law as an attempt to “appoint the State as the editor, curator and controller of online speech” and “override Meta’s editorial judgment about how to curate and display these billions of posts of third-party speech.”

According to The Associated Press , in TikTok’s filing, the company called the bill a “blatantly unconstitutional restriction on free expression that erodes the long-standing and protected practice of curating content based on user preferences, which bookstores, TV networks and streaming services all use.”

TikTok’s lawsuit went on to highlight the multiple safety measures it already has in place to protect young users.

Google, in its lawsuit , called on the state to defer restrictions on child social media usage to parents, referencing its own range of parental controls.

The legal challenge comes after tech company Meta, which owns Facebook and Instagram, along with Snapchat’s parent company Snap Inc. both settled lawsuits with teenagers alleging their platforms had adverse mental health effects. The two social media industry giants are also embroiled in a similar lawsuit in Los Angeles, in which plaintiffs allege their platforms are purposefully designed to be addictive.

Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg is expected to take the stand in this trial sometime in November.

The Los Angeles lawsuit targeted social media companies over the design of the platforms as opposed to the content.

Several tech industry leaders have agreed to multimillion dollar payouts to settle similar child online safety lawsuits.

In late August, Meta agreed to pay Texas more than $1 billion and pledged to add new restrictions to its platforms, such as blocking notifications during school hours and applying default daily time limits of two hours for users under the age of 18, which can only be lifted by a parent.
